stories.title: Apple caught off guard by AI demand for Mac Mini and Mac Studio
stories.blurb: Developers running local AI workloads are snapping up Mac Minis and Mac Studios faster than Apple anticipated, causing supply crunches. This is a direct signal that Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture has become the go-to for on-device AI — and it has major implications for anyone choosing their next dev machine. 496 comments worth of opinions on this one.

stories.title: I turned my security cameras into an automatic bird identification system
stories.blurb: A hands-on walkthrough of repurposing existing security camera infrastructure with BirdNET-Go, an open-source ML model, for automated bird species ID. It's a perfect template for any AI-on-the-edge home automation project. The same pattern — local model, existing camera feed, zero cloud dependency — applies to dozens of other use cases.

stories.title: Fastpotify
stories.blurb: A blazingly fast Spotify client that's stirring up 322 comments worth of debate. The HN crowd is divided between praising the performance gains and questioning the API terms-of-service implications. Worth a look if Spotify's own client has been driving you crazy.

stories.title: Playa Phone
stories.blurb: The top-scoring story today: Playa Phone is a browser-based music playground that lets you compose and share beats with a surprisingly deep sequencer. The highest score of the day points to something genuinely fun that's landed well with the HN crowd. Great for a creative afternoon detour.

stories.title: Smartphone LED detects hidden cameras with AI
stories.blurb: Researchers have developed a technique that uses a smartphone's LED flash plus an AI classifier to detect hidden camera lenses via retroreflectance — no special hardware required. For privacy-conscious travelers, this is a practical tool that could arrive as an app sooner than you think. The underlying technique is clever enough to warrant reading the details.

stories.title: I think the military commissary's freezers were hacked
stories.blurb: A gripping first-person account of suspicious freezer behavior at a military grocery store that points to a possible ICS/OT intrusion. It's a vivid reminder that critical infrastructure security extends to mundane devices like commercial refrigeration units. The Substack post reads like a security thriller with real-world stakes.

stories.title: AnkiDroid: Google Play no longer allowing Open Collective donation link
stories.blurb: Google is forcing AnkiDroid to remove its Open Collective donation link from the Play Store, citing payment policy — a policy that conveniently protects Google's own in-app purchase cut. This is an important open-source funding and platform control story that affects every developer distributing free apps on Android.

stories.title: GPU World
stories.blurb: GPU World is a live marketplace and comparison tracker for GPU compute — cloud instances, bare metal, spot pricing — all in one place. For anyone running LLM inference or training workloads, this is an immediately bookmarkable resource. The 172-comment thread is full of tips on where the real GPU bargains are right now.

stories.title: A walkable ASCII cyberpunk city in one HTML file [video]
stories.blurb: Someone crammed an explorable ASCII cyberpunk cityscape into a single HTML file — no frameworks, no dependencies, pure creative coding wizardry. It's a masterclass in constraint-driven creativity and a strong argument for what a single motivated developer can do with vanilla web tech. The video walkthrough is deeply satisfying.

stories.title: 44% on ARC-AGI-1 in 67 cents
stories.blurb: A developer achieved 44% on ARC-AGI-1 — a notoriously hard abstract reasoning benchmark — for just $0.67 in API costs using a clever prompting and sampling strategy. This is exactly the kind of scrappy prompt engineering result that matters for anyone trying to squeeze reasoning performance out of frontier models on a budget. The methodology is reproducible and well-documented.

stories.title: ChatGPT Work Tool and Skill Reference
stories.blurb: Simon Willison's structured reference for ChatGPT's built-in tools and capabilities — think of it as the missing manual for power users. If you're building AI workflows or just trying to get more out of ChatGPT's code interpreter, file search, and browsing tools, this is an immediately useful bookmark. Actionable today.

stories.title: We Let AI Agents Rewrite a 92M-Message-a-Day Service in Go
stories.blurb: Checkly's engineering team used AI coding agents to rewrite a high-throughput Node.js service in Go, documenting exactly what worked, what broke, and where humans had to intervene. It's one of the most concrete real-world accounts of agentic coding on production-scale systems yet published. Essential reading if you're evaluating Claude Code or similar tools for non-trivial rewrites.

stories.title: Run macOS Software on Linux
stories.blurb: Darling is a macOS compatibility layer for Linux — essentially Wine for macOS binaries, running Mach-O executables without a VM. For developers who need to test or run macOS-only tools in a Linux CI environment, this is a fascinating project to watch. The HN thread digs into where it currently succeeds and where it still falls short.

stories.title: RavynOS: Pre-alpha open-source OS based on Darwin, FreeBSD, Apple open-source
stories.blurb: RavynOS aims to be a free, open-source OS with macOS-compatible APIs and a familiar Aqua-inspired feel, built on FreeBSD and Apple's open-source components. It's pre-alpha and rough around the edges, but the ambition is remarkable for Apple ecosystem watchers. The 121-comment HN thread is a great discussion of the technical and legal challenges involved.

stories.title: EFF to Courts: Don't Rewrite Copyright over AI Hype
stories.blurb: The EFF is filing briefs urging courts not to bend existing copyright doctrine just to accommodate AI training lawsuits — arguing that bad precedent set now will haunt developers and researchers for decades. This is a must-read for anyone building with LLMs who cares about the legal ground beneath their feet. The EFF's framing of 'AI hype driving bad law' is pointed and persuasive.

stories.title: Reverse engineering my ADHD test
stories.blurb: A developer reverse-engineered the JavaScript of a commercial ADHD screening tool and found the scoring algorithm is embarrassingly simplistic — trivially gameable and scientifically dubious. It's a sharp piece of applied reverse engineering with real implications for anyone who's taken or been asked to take one of these assessments. The code analysis is meticulous.

stories.title: Cheap GPS jammers are filling the world with navigation dead zones
stories.blurb: Cheap consumer GPS jammers — originally sold to defeat fleet tracking — are proliferating globally and creating unpredictable navigation blackouts that affect aviation, shipping, and everyday drivers. The WSJ piece maps the scope of the problem with data, and the 164-comment HN thread gets into the RF physics and policy failures. A slow-motion infrastructure crisis.

stories.title: Dwarf Fortress is getting the mother of all magic updates
stories.blurb: Dwarf Fortress's upcoming magic system overhaul is so ambitious it reworks the fundamental cosmological rules of each generated world — think procedurally generated metaphysics. The RPS writeup captures the sheer scale of what Bay 12 Games is attempting, and it's a reminder that some of the most interesting game design is still happening outside the AAA mainstream. The 186 HN comments are a love letter to simulation depth.

stories.title: Terence Tao explains 6 essential mathematical concepts [video]
stories.blurb: The world's greatest living mathematician walks through six fundamental mathematical ideas in an accessible video format. Even developers who don't touch pure math daily will find Tao's explanations sharpening their intuition for abstraction and proof. Bookmark this for a lunch-break that makes you smarter.

stories.title: Evidence of Fraud in an Influential Study About Procrastination
stories.blurb: The DataColada team has uncovered statistical evidence of data fabrication in a widely-cited procrastination research paper — the kind that fed decades of self-help advice and workplace productivity frameworks. It's a meticulous forensic takedown that raises serious questions about what we think we know about motivation science. The replication crisis claims another scalp.
